notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Proverbs 23. Most of it comes from Enduring Word (David Guzik), the Pulpit Commentary, the NET Bible notes and the older commentaries collected on Bible Hub. I wasn't able to read the full chapter at Enduring Word (the page cut off after v. 21) or Constable's notes (only search excerpts). So the points for vv. 22–35 rely more on those excerpts and the NET notes.

**Gaps:**
- **Tradition differences:** I found only one real split between teachers, on the "rod" in vv. 13–14. I found no tradition-labelled debate on wine (vv. 29–35).
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I found only translation differences, nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Prosperity and other popular teaching:** I found nothing on this chapter.

I've left these areas out rather than filling them in from my own knowledge.

---

**Background (vv. 1–35)**
- These verses belong to a section that NET says is very similar in style to Egypt's Instruction of Amenemope, "especially the thirty precepts of the sages in 22:17–24:22". https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?amp=&amp=&book=Pro&chapter=22&verse=17
- Guzik thinks "it is likely that Solomon patterned this section after the Egyptian wisdom writing Amenemope." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-22.cfm
- GotQuestions sets out three positions. Some scholars think the Egyptian text shaped the Hebrew one, others think the reverse, and still others think the link is coincidental. https://www.gotquestions.org/Instruction-of-Amenemope.html
- Guzik reads the chapter as a father's warnings about wealth, food, foolishness, sexual sin and alcohol. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/

**v. 1**
- Guzik pictures a generous invitation to a powerful person's table, and compares Daniel 1. His warning is not to be won over by the atmosphere of power and luxury. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/
- Translation question: the Pulpit Commentary says the phrase can also mean "who is before you." Then the guest should watch the host, a superior who can raise him up or ruin him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- Constable prefers "what is before you." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-23.html
- NET calls vv. 1–3 the sixth saying, about caution before rulers, and compares Amenemope ch. 23. "One should not get too familiar with rulers, for they always have ulterior motives." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23
- Older reading: the Pulpit Commentary notes that earlier commentators used these verses as a lesson on reverently taking Holy Communion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm

**v. 2**
- NET: "put a knife to your throat" is an idiom for curbing your appetite. It comes from a time of all-powerful tyrants, when indulging yourself before one was very risky. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23
- Barnes: eat as if a knife were at your throat. Others read it as "indulging at such a time could cost you your life." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/23-2.htm
- Guzik quotes Waltke: total abstinence is needed for anyone who cannot control his appetites, and this applies to every appetite (Matt. 5:29–30). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: such meals are often offered not out of friendship but to get a man to expose himself, his character or his secrets. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- Guzik: at the ruler's table you might give up what should not be given up, or promise what should not be promised. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Proverbs mocks laziness, but work and wealth must not become idols. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/
- Pulpit: the "wisdom" to stop is *binah*, the practical cleverness used for making money. It is not the highest kind of wisdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- Chuck Smith links it to Ps. 62:10: God may increase riches, just don't set your heart on them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/proverbs-23.html

**v. 5**
- NET: the Hebrew is hard; the sense is that just when you think you are close, wealth slips away. Amenemope has a similar line about riches growing wings like geese. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23
- Guzik quotes Waltke: once riches are gone, they are gone forever. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/

**v. 6**
- NET: the "evil eye" is the opposite of the "good eye" of the generous man. It means someone out to get everything for himself. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23
- Chuck Smith: the phrase is not about the superstition of casting a hex. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/proverbs-23.html

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew verb means "to calculate." The stingy host watches every bite and resents it. (This is behind the KJV's "as he thinketh in his heart, so is he.") https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- NET: the Greek translation (LXX) reads "hair" instead, giving the picture of a hair stuck in the throat. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23
- The Restoration Commentary links it to Rom. 12:9 (love without hypocrisy), as a warning not to be this kind of host ourselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/proverbs-23.html

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: you would owe no thanks for food given so grudgingly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- NET: the line is deliberate exaggeration; the whole experience turns your stomach. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: the "fool" (*kesil*) is the dull, stubborn man. Speaking to him is like throwing pearls before pigs (Matt. 7:6). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- Constable adds that God can still change people's minds about wisdom. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-23.html
- NET: Egyptian literature has no direct parallel to this saying. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23

**vv. 10–11**
- Guzik: moving a boundary stone was a way to steal land. Symbolically it can also stand for inherited tradition. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/
- Pulpit: the "Redeemer" (*goel*) was the near relative who defended a family member. Here God himself is the orphans' *goel*. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: wisdom has to be actively received, with both heart and ears. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/
- Constable: v. 12 is probably the close of the tenth saying, though some see it as an introduction to the rest. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-23.html

**vv. 13–14 (the "rod")**
- Guzik: the rod is sometimes literal (such as spanking) and sometimes figurative. He quotes Waltke: parents who brutalize their children cannot hide behind Proverbs. He also cites Garrett pointing to Eph. 6:4. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/
- Pulpit: "he will not die" just means don't hold back from fear of hurting the child. Sheol here means early death, and also spiritual death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- NET: Sheol here probably means "death," not the realm of departed spirits. A similar saying appears in the Aramaic wisdom book of Ahiqar. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23
- Where teachers differ:
  - **Sam Storms** (on your charismatic list): the "rod" need not mean an object; it is a way of referring to discipline. He also warns against using the rod without words. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/loving-and-leading-our-children-through-discipline---proverbs-1324
  - **Bob Deffinbaugh** (bible.org, evangelical): nearly every "rod" in Proverbs could be translated "spanking," but it is not the only form of correction. https://bible.org/seriespage/16-wisdom-and-child-rearing-part-iii
  - **Chuck Smith**: children have different temperaments, so find other forms of discipline where spanking doesn't work. He says he doesn't believe Scripture supports child-beating. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/proverbs-23.html

**vv. 15–16**
- Pulpit: "reins" (kidneys) were seen as the seat of feeling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- NET: the four lines mirror each other (wise heart / joy / joy / right words). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23
- Constable: the affectionate "my son" removes any idea that the father enjoyed punishing. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-23.html

**v. 17**
- Pulpit and NET: the same Hebrew verb means "envy" toward sinners and "zeal" toward the fear of the LORD. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon defining the fear of the LORD as true religion: reverence, awe and childlike trust. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: the writer believes in a future life that will put right all unfairness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- NET: the line is an understatement; the hope will actually be fulfilled. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23

**v. 19**
- Pulpit: "the way" is the one right path, as opposed to the many wrong ones. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- Matthew Henry: if the heart is guided, the steps will be too. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/23.htm

**vv. 20–21**
- NET: the Hebrew means "drunkards," which is stronger than "those who drink too much." The Mishnah uses drunkenness and gluttony to identify a rebellious son. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=23
- Pulpit: Jesus was accused of being exactly this pair, a glutton and a drunkard (Matt. 11:19). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- Guzik quotes Waltke: full stomachs empty their minds. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/

**v. 22**
- Guzik: this applies "honor your father and mother" (Exod. 20:12; Eph. 6:2); elderly parents deserve special care. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/

**v. 23**
- Matthew Henry: give up anything for truth, and don't trade it for pleasure, honour or riches. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/23.htm
- NET: the Hebrew says "buy." "Getting truth" means being trained in it. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=pro&chapter=23&verse=23

**vv. 24–25**
- Constable: here "righteous" and "wise" mean the same thing. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-23.html
- The Restoration Commentary links it to the Father's joy in Jesus (Matt. 3:17). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/proverbs-23.html

**v. 26**
- Guzik: at least at the time of writing, Solomon could point to his own life as an example. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/
- The Restoration Commentary agrees with Deane that Wisdom herself is speaking here (Toy disagrees). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/proverbs-23.html
- Matthew Henry: God wants the whole heart, "all or none." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/proverbs/23.htm

**v. 27**
- NET: the "pit" and "narrow well" picture a trap with no way out, a doorway to Sheol. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Pro&chapter=23&verse=27

**v. 28**
- Guzik: this doesn't put all the blame on the woman, but her trap catches many. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/
- NET rejects Dahood's suggestion that the word means "garments" as far-fetched. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Pro&chapter=23&verse=28

**vv. 29–30**
- NET: v. 29 is a riddle about drunkenness, and v. 30 gives the answer. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+23%3A29-35
- Guzik quotes Waltke: putting the warnings about the seductress and wine side by side is deliberate, because both are hidden, deadly traps. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-23/

**v. 31**
- Poole and Benson: the ban is on looking with longing, as with looking at a woman (Matt. 5:28). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/23-31.htm
- Gill: it isn't unlawful to look at wine, only to look at it greedily. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/23-31.htm
- Clarke aims the warning at someone already addicted, who has no self-control. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/proverbs/23-31.html
- Catholic translation note: the Douay-Rheims has "yellow," and Pulpit traces this to the Latin Vulgate. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/23-31.htm

**v. 32**
- NET: the Hebrew says "its end." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+23%3A29-35

**v. 33**
- Pulpit keeps the KJV reading "strange women," linking drunkenness and lust. Ewald and Delitzsch read "strange things" (hallucinations) instead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
- NET reads "strange things": trouble seeing and speaking. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+23%3A29-35

**v. 34**
- NET: being drunk is compared to being seasick, tossed about at sea or up on the rigging. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+23%3A29-35

**v. 35**
- NET: the drunk doesn't feel or remember the beating, and wants another drink. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Pro+23:31-35
- Pulpit: a treatise on conscience attached to St. Bernard's works applies this to a conscience hardened by habit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/23.htm
